anchor: many and many a year ago
title: Publication and occasion
short: Poe's last completed poem, written about May 1849 and first printed two days after his death, inside Griswold's hostile obituary.
body: Poe made several fair copies in mid-1849 (for Griswold, John Moore, Henry Hirst, John Sartain and, on 26 September, John R. Thompson), and the Poe Society lists six primary printings and dozens of newspaper reprints in 1849-50. The Tribune text of 9 October 1849, in Rufus Griswold's obituary two days after Poe died in Baltimore, is probably the first to reach readers (the Society also records Richmond Examiner proofs of about September 1849); the first authorised printing was in Sartain's Union Magazine, January 1850. Mabbott's edition prints two texts (from the Griswold and Thompson manuscripts) because the copies differ in small but telling ways. The opening is a storyteller's formula, the 'once upon a time' of fairy tale and ballad, which sets the love outside ordinary history.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, 'Annabel Lee': manuscripts, printings and texts
New-York Daily Tribune, 9 October 1849, p. 2 (Griswold's 'Ludwig' obituary), transcription at eapoe.org
T. O. Mabbott, ed., Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. 1: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'Annabel Lee', introduction and notes

anchor: In a kingdom by the sea
title: Metre, stanza and refrain
short: A ballad in loose anapaestic lines, long and short lines alternating, with refrain words returning in every stanza.
body: The lines run mostly in triple rhythm (da-da-DUM), alternating four-beat and three-beat lines as in ballad measure, but the stanzas lengthen irregularly (six, six, eight, six, seven and eight lines). One rhyme sound dominates: 'sea' and 'Lee' with 'me' and 'we' end nearly every short line, so the poem sounds like a single incantation. Poe had argued in 'The Philosophy of Composition' (1846) that a refrain gains force when the sound stays the same while its application varies; here 'kingdom by the sea' moves from fairy-tale setting to the place of death to the site of the tomb. The Sartain manuscript is titled 'Annabel Lee: A Ballad', which confirms the genre Poe had in mind.

sources.cite: Poe, 'The Philosophy of Composition', Graham's Magazine, April 1846
T. O. Mabbott, ed., Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. 1: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'Annabel Lee', introduction and notes
Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, 'Annabel Lee': manuscripts, printings and texts

title: 'kingdom by the sea'
short: A dream geography, not a real place: a romance kingdom whose sea marks the edge of the world and of death.
body: The phrase recurs five times and changes its weight each time. Biographers have tried to locate it (Charleston and Sullivan's Island, where Poe served as a soldier, or the Baltimore of Virginia's girlhood), but Mabbott and most critics prefer to read it as an imagined space, like the 'misty mid region of Weir' in 'Ulalume'. The sea in Poe is often a boundary between the living and the dead, as in 'The City in the Sea'. By the last stanza the speaker lies 'by the side of the sea', and the kingdom has shrunk to a tomb.

sources.cite: T. O. Mabbott, ed., Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. 1: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'Annabel Lee', introduction and notes

title: Annabel Lee
short: The name is chosen for its liquid sounds; who stood behind it was disputed from the start.
body: Like 'Lenore' and 'Ulalume', the name is built from l, n and open vowels, the sounds Poe valued for melancholy. Several women claimed to be the original: Sarah Helen Whitman, Frances Sargent Osgood, Estelle Anna Lewis, and his first sweetheart Elmira Royster (by 1849 the widowed Mrs Shelton, to whom he was then engaged). Most biographers, including Quinn and Silverman, think first of his wife Virginia Clemm, who married him at thirteen and died of tuberculosis in January 1847. Mabbott warned that the figure is imaginary and that no single model should be pressed. The capitals reproduce the typography of the archive's source text.

sources.cite: T. O. Mabbott, ed., Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. 1: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'Annabel Lee', introduction and notes

title: Child lovers
short: The love is placed in childhood, which makes it innocent, absolute and outside adult society.
body: Readers have linked the line to Virginia, Poe's cousin, whom he married in 1836 when she was thirteen. But the motif of child-lovers is also literary, part of the Romantic idealisation of first love. Some critics take the speaker's explanation of her death (the envy of the angels) as itself childish, a sign that the speaker has never grown beyond the loss. Others read the insistence on childhood as shielding the love from sexuality, which the closing image of a bride in a sepulchre then complicates.

title: seraphs
short: The highest order of angels, from Isaiah's vision; here they behave like jealous rivals.
body: In Isaiah 6:2 the seraphim stand above the throne of God, each with six wings. Christian angelology (pseudo-Dionysius) ranked them first among the nine orders, burning with love of God. Poe turns this upside down: the angels who should embody perfect love are the ones who 'coveted' a human love. A related idea appears in Poe's 'Israfel' (1831), where the speaker imagines changing places with an angel. The English plural 'seraphs', instead of Hebrew 'seraphim', was common in the period.

title: Coveted
short: To covet is the sin forbidden in the Tenth Commandment, so heaven itself is accused of sin.
body: 'Thou shalt not covet' (Exodus 20:17) forbids desiring what belongs to a neighbour. By giving the verb to the seraphs Poe makes the angels guilty of envy, one of the seven deadly sins, and the speaker's grief becomes a charge against heaven. The verb opens a short line of its own, which isolates the accusation. The theme returns in stanza 4, 'Went envying her and me', where the reason is stated a second time with emphatic certainty.

anchor: blew out of a cloud, chilling
title: The chilling wind
short: Death comes as a cold wind from the sky, often read as a veiled image of fever or consumption.
body: The cause of death is natural and supernatural at once: a wind from a cloud, sent (the speaker believes) by envious angels. Readers who take Virginia as the model connect the chill with the tuberculosis that killed her after years of illness, with repeated haemorrhages and fevers that Poe's letters describe. The line ends on the falling word 'chilling', and in stanza 4 the word returns paired with its rhyme, 'Chilling and killing', the climax of the poem's internal rhyming.

title: 'highborn kinsmen'
short: Who are the kinsmen? Her noble relatives, or the angels themselves come to claim her soul?
body: Read literally, the 'highborn kinsmen' are her aristocratic family, who part the lovers as in a ballad of feuding houses and bury her. But 'highborn' can be heard as 'born on high', and many readers take them to be the seraphs, now acting as her heavenly kin and carrying her off. The ambiguity suits the poem's double world: the same event is a funeral on earth and an abduction by heaven. Hoffman reads kinsmen and angels alike as figures of everything that intrudes on the closed world of the couple.

anchor: shut her up in a sepulchre
title: sepulchre
short: A tomb, especially a stone burial chamber; the word carries biblical and Gothic associations.
body: The word is the King James term for the tomb of Christ (Matthew 27:60), which lends the burial solemnity. 'Shut her up' suggests imprisonment, as if the family had locked away a living girl; Poe's fiction often dwells on burial alive ('The Fall of the House of Usher', 'The Premature Burial'). The sepulchre returns in the final stanza, where the speaker lies down beside it every night.

anchor: not half so happy in heaven
title: 'not half so happy'
short: The angels are less happy in heaven than the lovers on earth; many reprints read 'so merry'.
body: The claim is bold theology: earthly love surpasses heavenly bliss. The Poe Society notes that many reprints substitute 'so merry in Heaven' for 'so happy in Heaven', a variant students will meet in anthologies. The following parenthesis, '(as all men know', is a rhetorical bluff that claims common knowledge for a private conviction, and the dashes and 'Yes!' make the speaker's voice more agitated than in the opening stanzas.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, 'Annabel Lee': manuscripts, printings and texts

anchor: Chilling and killing my ANNABEL LEE
title: 'Chilling and killing'
short: An internal rhyme that turns the earlier 'chilling' into death outright.
body: Stanza 3 had ended a line on 'chilling'; now the word is paired with 'killing' inside a single line. The device is typical of Poe's late style ('The Raven', 'Ulalume', 'The Bells') and of his belief, set out in 'The Poetic Principle', that music lies close to the essence of poetry. The jingle is the poem's first plain statement that she died, delivered in a sound almost like a nursery rhyme, which makes it all the more disturbing.

sources.cite: Poe, 'The Poetic Principle' (lecture 1848-49; printed 1850)

title: Older and wiser
short: The speaker sets the lovers against the old and wise: love, not experience, is the higher knowledge.
body: The two lines beginning 'Of' rhyme on 'we' and run on into the 'sea' and 'Lee' rhymes that close the stanza. The contrast between child-lovers and older, wiser people repeats the poem's claim that this love was 'more than love'. Critics divide over whether this is Romantic defiance (love stronger than death, as in the Song of Songs 8:6, 'love is strong as death') or a grieving man's refusal to accept adult reality.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Song of Solomon 8:6

anchor: the demons down under the sea
title: Angels and demons
short: Heaven above and demons below form a cosmic frame: nothing in the universe can part their souls.
body: The pairing recalls Romans 8:38-39, where neither death nor life nor angels can separate the faithful from the love of God; Poe transfers the promise to human lovers. The demons under the sea give the 'kingdom by the sea' a hell beneath it. Critics have noted that, unlike 'The Raven', whose speaker's soul shall be lifted 'nevermore', this poem insists on the lovers' union beyond death.

title: dissever
greek: Latin dis- + separare, via Old French dessevrer
short: To part or sever completely; a formal, slightly archaic word chosen also for its rhyme with 'ever'.
body: The OED records 'dissever' from Middle English in the sense of separating or dividing. Poe uses it for its weight and for its chime with 'ever', another internal rhyme. The claim that soul cannot be parted from soul is the poem's thesis, and it prepares for the final stanza, where the dead woman's presence is felt every night through the moon and stars.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'dissever'

title: 'night-tide' and the internal rhymes
short: 'Night-tide' means night-time, with a pun on the tide of the sea beside which he lies.
body: 'Tide' in the old sense of time or season (as in 'eventide' and 'Christmastide') gives 'night-tide', the whole night; the sea setting adds the second sense of a tide that rises and falls. The last stanza is crowded with internal rhymes (beams/dreams, rise/eyes, night-tide/side, life/bride), so the music thickens as the speaker approaches the tomb. Some texts print the word without a hyphen.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'tide'

title: 'my life and my bride'
short: The speaker lies down beside the dead woman as her bridegroom, an image read as devotion or as morbid obsession.
body: Poe's own theory held that the death of a beautiful woman is, as he put it, 'the most poetical topic in the world' ('The Philosophy of Composition'). The ending takes that idea to its limit: the lover sleeps beside the tomb each night. Marie Bonaparte's psychoanalytic study (1933) read such poems as necrophile fantasy rooted in the early loss of Poe's mother; later critics such as Hoffman see a worship that becomes possible only once the beloved is dead. Others read 'bride' as simple conjugal fidelity beyond death.

anchor: by the side of the sea
title: The last line and its variant
short: The archive follows the reading 'by the side of the sea' (the Thompson manuscript of September 1849); earlier fair copies read 'by the sounding sea'.
body: The final line is the most famous variant in the poem. The Poe Society's comparative text shows that the first four fair copies of 1849 (Griswold, Moore, Hirst, Sartain) read 'In her tomb by the sounding sea', a conventional poetic epithet, and Sartain's Union Magazine printed that reading in January 1850. Poe's last manuscript, the Thompson copy of 26 September 1849, reads 'In her tomb by the side of the sea', which repeats 'side' from two lines before and keeps the flat, exhausted cadence of grief. Mabbott prints both the Griswold and Thompson texts, so the reading a student meets depends on the edition.

sources.cite: Edgar Allan Poe Society of Baltimore, 'Annabel Lee': comparative text of the five 1849 manuscripts
T. O. Mabbott, ed., Collected Works of Edgar Allan Poe, vol. 1: Poems (Harvard UP, 1969), 'Annabel Lee', introduction and notes
